episode.broadcastScript:
This is The Innovation Pulse for the week ending Friday, May twenty-second, twenty twenty-six. And here's who is innovating in higher education this week.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Leading off this week's Innovation Pulse, artificial intelligence has crossed a historic threshold. OpenAI's GPT-4.5 was judged to be human seventy-three percent of the time in controlled Turing test experiments, a UC San Diego study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences found. The actual humans in the same experiments were judged to be human only fifty-four percent of the time.

The study is the first to rigorously test large language models using the framework that British mathematician Alan Turing created in nineteen fifty. Across randomized experiments with undergraduates and online participants, GPT-4.5 fooled interrogators nearly three-quarters of the time. Meta's LLaMa model was judged human fifty-six percent of the time, statistically indistinguishable from real humans.

Cameron Jones, the study's corresponding author, said that with the right prompts, advanced large language models can exhibit the same tone, directness, humor, and fallibility as humans. The key factor was persona prompting. Without explicit instructions telling the model how to behave like a human, success rates dropped from seventy-three to thirty-six percent.

Study co-author Ben Bergen noted that the models won by making mistakes, using humor, and displaying social traits rather than by demonstrating superior knowledge. Quote, People should be much less confident that they know they're talking to a human when interacting with strangers online today, Jones said.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In research news, a multimodal surgical agent developed at the University of Miami's Desai Sethi Urology Institute reduced operative documentation time by seventy percent in live clinical deployment. Dr. Archan Khandekar reported the findings at the American Urological Association's twenty twenty-six Annual Meeting.

The system cut operative note completion time from approximately twenty-six minutes to under two minutes per case by integrating computer vision, robotic video analysis, and electronic health record systems. Surgeons averaged only six edits per case. In research applications, the agent reproduced a previously published peer-reviewed study on warm ischemia time across sixty-one cases in three minutes and twenty-six seconds, achieving greater than ninety-five percent concordance with original findings that required weeks to complete.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Also in research, an A.I.-powered CPR coaching tool significantly outperformed 911 dispatchers in guiding bystanders through resuscitation steps, JAMA Internal Medicine published this week. University of California San Diego researchers developed the tool and tested it against recordings of twelve real emergency calls.

The A.I. coach achieved perfect scores on basic CPR steps, while dispatchers scored eighty-five percent. The gap widened for advanced techniques, with the A.I. scoring ninety-nine percent compared to dispatchers' sixty-three percent. Only two percent of Americans are CPR-certified while more than three hundred fifty thousand suffer out-of-hospital cardiac arrest annually with survival rates around nine percent. The tool is available open-source for public use.

<break time="1.0s"/>

At the University of Louisville, researchers are now running A.I. models that autonomously decide which laboratory experiments to conduct. Associate Professor Badri Narayanan said the A.I. handles most of the heavy lifting in his materials science research, with autonomous experimentation capabilities that could compress commercial battery development from ten to fifteen years down to just three to four years.

The Zurada computing system, named after neural networks pioneer Professor Jacek Zurada, supports the approach with forty-three NVIDIA GPUs and over one point six petaflops of computing power. Medical researchers on the platform are developing individualized treatment tools for chronic kidney disease and eating disorders.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In Insights and Trends, more than half of special education teachers now use A.I. tools to develop individualized education plans, up from thirty-nine percent just one year ago. The Center for Democracy and Technology survey documents the rapid adoption shift as forty-five states report ongoing special education teacher shortages.

Mary Acebu at Riverview Middle School in Bay Point, California, previously spent forty-five minutes developing three to four I.E.P. goals per student. Using district-vetted tools, she now completes that work faster. Her colleague Paul Stone, a twenty-two-year teaching veteran who was initially skeptical, now calls the technology an amazing time-saver. However, the Center for Democracy and Technology notes that student privacy remains the primary concern, and potential A.I. bias against people with disabilities poses ethical challenges.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Meanwhile at UC Berkeley, students earned thirty percent more A grades in courses with writing and coding assignments after ChatGPT launched compared to students in the same courses before the tool became available. Researcher Igor Chirikov analyzed more than three hundred courses across eighty-four departments from twenty eighteen through twenty twenty-five, examining more than five hundred thousand student enrollments. The grade increases were largest in courses where homework counted more heavily toward the final grade. Chirikov found that A.I. primarily converted A-minus and B-plus grades into A grades. The analysis showed that struggling students did not improve their performance. Quote, the results suggest that students have relied on generative A.I. to do better in their studies, not that these classes of students are learning more, Chirikov said. Employers responded to the grade inflation by increasing GPA requirements. On Handshake, the share of job postings requiring a three point five GPA or higher jumped from nine percent in twenty twenty to twenty-five percent in twenty twenty-six.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In A.I. Workforce and Careers news, A.T. and T. cannot find enough workers who know electricity and photonics to install and maintain the fiber optic networks carrying data across the country. CEO John Stankey told CNBC this week that the company needs electricians and fiber optic technicians for infrastructure that A.I. cannot install or maintain itself.

Entry-level hiring at the telecommunications giant has slowed for college graduates in marketing, legal services, accounting, human resources, and IT departments. Ford and other large employers are making the same shift toward skilled trades workers. On job platform Handshake, postings seeking electricians and technicians have increased while postings for entry-level corporate roles requiring four-year degrees have declined markedly.

<break time="1.0s"/>

City Colleges of Chicago is one of five institutions nationwide selected as regional leads for Amazon Web Services Machine Learning University. The designation brings free cloud computing infrastructure and ready-to-teach A.I. curriculum to the seven-campus system.

Students gain no-cost access to the same database, A.I., and machine learning tools that A.W.S. professionals use. Faculty receive bootcamp training, lecture slides, coding exercises, and instructor handbooks designed for college-level, for-credit courses. Four inaugural faculty fellows will lead regional workshops extending the program to other Midwest community colleges and H.B.C.U.s.

The regional lead model is replicable. A.W.S. selected Howard University, Delaware State University, Alabama A. and M. University, and Oklahoma City Community College as the four other regional leads. Community college systems seeking similar resources can pursue the same pathway through A.W.S. Machine Learning University's educator consortium. The initiative includes student business case competitions alongside faculty development.

<break time="1.0s"/>

And in a development affecting academic integrity policies, A.I. detection tools flagged human-written student work as machine-generated while missing actual A.I.-generated text in controlled testing, a CNET investigation this month found. The pattern of accuracy problems has prompted institutions to reconsider their verification methods.

Students at multiple institutions faced misconduct charges based on incorrect detection scores. The students who challenged the accusations presented drafts, notes, and revision history demonstrating their writing process over time. All of the appeals were successful. In controlled comparisons, human evaluators who had studied common A.I. writing patterns identified machine-generated text more consistently than the automated systems did. Several institutions have now stopped using detection software as primary evidence in academic integrity cases.

<break time="1.0s"/>

That's this week's Innovation Pulse. Full coverage and source links at innovating higher ed dot com.

leadStory.headline: A.I. Can Now Pass the Turing Test
leadStory.summary: OpenAI's GPT-4.5 was judged to be human seventy-three percent of the time in controlled Turing test experiments, a UC San Diego study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences found. The actual humans in the same experiments were judged to be human only fifty-four percent of the time. The study is the first to rigorously test large language models using the framework that British mathematician Alan Turing created in 1950. The test requires a human interrogator to chat simultaneously with two parties — one human, one machine — and then determine which is which. Across randomized experiments with UC San Diego undergraduates and online participants, GPT-4.5 fooled interrogators nearly three-quarters of the time. Meta's LLaMa-3.1-405B was judged human fifty-six percent of the time, a rate statistically indistinguishable from real humans in the experiments. Older systems like ELIZA and GPT-4o scored between twenty-one and twenty-three percent. Cameron Jones, the study's corresponding author, said that with the right prompts, advanced LLMs can exhibit the same tone, directness, humor, and fallibility as humans. The key factor was persona prompting — explicit instructions telling the A.I. how to behave like a human. Without those instructions, GPT-4.5's success rate dropped from seventy-three to thirty-six percent. Study co-author Ben Bergen, a cognitive science professor at UC San Diego, noted that the models won by making mistakes, using humor, and displaying social traits rather than by demonstrating superior knowledge. Jones said people should be much less confident that they know they're talking to a human when interacting with strangers online today.

quickHits.headline: AI Surgical Agent Cuts Documentation Time 70 Percent
quickHits.summary:
A multimodal A.I. surgical agent developed at the University of Miami's Desai Sethi Urology Institute reduced operative documentation time by 70 percent in live clinical deployment. Dr. Archan Khandekar, assistant professor of urologic oncology, reported the findings at the American Urological Association's 2026 Annual Meeting.

The A.I. system cut operative note completion time from approximately 26 minutes to under 2 minutes per case by integrating computer vision, robotic operative video analysis, and electronic health record systems. Surgeons averaged only 6 edits per case, primarily correcting artery versus vein labeling.

In research applications, the A.I. agent reproduced a previously published peer-reviewed study on warm ischemia time across 61 robotic partial nephrectomy cases in 3 minutes and 26 seconds, achieving greater than 95 percent concordance with original findings that required weeks to complete.

Safety testing showed grounded language models scored 24 to 25 of 25 on clinical guidelines compliance, while ungrounded models produced clinically dangerous errors. The technology currently operates in UHealth facilities.

quickHits.headline: AI CPR Coach Outperforms 911 Dispatchers in Guiding Bystanders
quickHits.summary:
An A.I.-powered CPR coaching tool significantly outperformed 911 dispatchers in guiding bystanders through resuscitation steps, according to research published in JAMA Internal Medicine. University of California San Diego researchers developed ChatCPR and tested it against recordings of 12 real emergency calls.

The A.I. coach achieved perfect scores on basic CPR steps, while dispatchers scored 85 percent on the same measures. The performance gap widened for advanced techniques, with ChatCPR scoring 99 percent compared to dispatchers' 63 percent.

Lead author Nimit Desai, a medical student and research affiliate at UC San Diego's Qualcomm Institute, worked with teams from University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine and Johns Hopkins University. The researchers first benchmarked six major A.I. models on CPR instruction before developing their specialized tool.

Only 2 percent of Americans are CPR-certified while more than 350,000 suffer out-of-hospital cardiac arrest annually with survival rates around 9 percent. The ChatCPR tool is available open-source for public use.

quickHits.summary:

Research from the University of Virginia and University of Central Florida found A.I.-assisted I.E.P.s matched or exceeded teacher-only quality.
